 418	func (c *Coder) displayName(abs string) string {
 419		rel := c.relFname(abs)
 420		up, rest := 0, rel
 421		for {
 422			if rest == ".." {
 423				up++
 424				rest = ""
 425				break
 426			}
 427			if !strings.HasPrefix(rest, "../") {
 428				break
 429			}
 430			up++
 431			rest = rest[len("../"):]
 432		}
 433		// rest == "" is the project's parent directory itself, which is not a file
 434		// anyone pins; it falls through to the absolute form rather than being
 435		// named "..".
 436		if up == 0 || (up == 1 && rest != "") {
 437			return rel
 438		}
 439		// Native separators, not ToSlash. A root-relative name is the tool-facing
 440		// form — read, grep, and ls all report forward slashes, and it has to match
 441		// them. An absolute name is not in that world: it is a path outside the
 442		// project, which the user will read, copy, and paste somewhere else, so it
 443		// should look the way their OS spells one. CI caught the difference as
 444		// C:/Users/... where Windows means C:\Users\...
 445		return filepath.Clean(abs)
 446	}

 494	// confirmGrouped wraps c.Confirm with group-scoped auto-approve. If the user
 495	// answered "a" to a previous Confirm with the same Group, this one is approved
 496	// without prompting. The first "a" answer records the group and returns true.
 497	// req.GroupSession picks how long the record lasts — the session, or the turn.

 499	// c.Confirm.Confirm directly.

 501	// Both maps are read on every call regardless of scope. A group is only ever
 502	// written to one of them, so this cannot widen a grant; what it does is keep a
 503	// session grant honored by a request that forgot to set GroupSession.
 504	func (c *Coder) confirmGrouped(req ConfirmRequest) bool {
 505		if req.Group != "" && (c.turnAutoApprove[req.Group] || c.sessionAutoApprove[req.Group]) {
 506			return true
 507		}
 508		res := c.Confirm.Confirm(req)
 509		if res.Always && req.Group != "" {
 510			if req.GroupSession {
 511				c.sessionAutoApprove[req.Group] = true
 512			} else {
 513				c.turnAutoApprove[req.Group] = true
 514			}
 515		}
 516		return res.Yes || res.Always

 519	// Run executes one scripted message (script mode) and returns the turn's
 520	// answer: every interrupted send's content in order, each steer as a
 521	// blockquote, and the final send's content — the same string the transcript
 522	// records.
 523	//
 524	// A panic inside the turn is recovered once, handed to OnCrash, and re-raised:
 525	// the transcript keeps the turn's partial answer (the caller appends its tool
 526	// lines and edited files from the same accessors it uses after a normal turn —
 527	// the panic unwound through runOne's defer, which settled those), and the
 528	// process still dies with the original stack trace. A recovered-and-swallowed
 529	// panic in a coding agent leaves the tree half-edited and the session running
 530	// on a broken coder; dying is the honest outcome. What recovery buys is that
 531	// the work the turn already did is not lost with the process.
 532	func (c *Coder) Run(ctx context.Context, withMessage string) (answer string) {
 533		defer func() {
 534			if r := recover(); r != nil {
 535				if c.OnCrash != nil {
 536					c.OnCrash(c.turnHistory + c.multiResponseContent + c.partialResponseContent)
 537				}
 538				panic(r)
 539			}
 540		}()
 541		c.runOne(ctx, withMessage)
 542		return c.turnHistory + c.multiResponseContent + c.partialResponseContent
 543	}

 545	// runOne is the turn loop. It keeps sending while the model has something to
 546	// react to — a tool result it hasn't seen (OutcomeContinue) or a mistake to fix
 547	// (OutcomeReflect) — and stops when the model has nothing left to say, the
 548	// human interrupts, or a budget is spent. The turn boundary is still the
 549	// human's: nothing here starts new work of its own.
 550	func (c *Coder) runOne(ctx context.Context, userMessage string) {
 551		c.initBeforeMessage()
 552		c.turnHistory = ""
 553	
 554		if userMessage == "" {
 555			return
 556		}
 557		message := userMessage
 558	
 559		// Committing and rotating settled history are both turn-end concerns.
 560		// Mid-loop the tool results must stay in cur, and summarizing them away
 561		// between steps would compact the very results the next send reacts to;
 562		// committing mid-loop would spend one commit per send on fragments of one
 563		// change. A defer covers every exit — budget declined, reflection cap,
 564		// interrupted, or done. An interrupted turn's edits are real, so they are
 565		// committed too.
 566		defer func() {
 567			c.settleEdits("")
 568			c.endTurnHistory()
 569			// Last, so the accounting closes the turn: the commit line above it, and
 570			// nothing under it. This is what the per-send reorder was reaching for,
 571			// now at the scope where a reader actually wants the number. Once per
 572			// turn even when the turn was steered, because a steered turn is still
 573			// one turn's spend.
 574			c.flushTurnUsage()
 575		}()
 576	
 577		// Outcome-driven so a re-send that carries no message text — both a tool
 578		// reflection and a tool continuation re-enter on the appended tool results
 579		// — keeps the loop going.
 580		for {
 581			outcome, reflection := c.sendSteerable(ctx, message)
 582			// After the send, not during it: sendMessage does its interrupt
 583			// handling before returning, and that handling can retract messages.
 584			c.recordNewMessages()
 585			c.lastSendOutcome = outcome
 586	
 587			switch outcome {
 588			case OutcomeReflect:
 589				if c.numReflections >= c.MaxErrorReflections {
 590					c.Out.Warningf("Only %d reflections allowed, stopping.", c.MaxErrorReflections)
 591					return
 592				}
 593				c.numReflections++
 594				message = reflection
 595	
 596			case OutcomeContinue:
 597				c.numSteps++
 598				if c.numSteps >= c.MaxSteps && !c.confirmMoreSteps() {
 599					return
 600				}
 601				message = "" // the tool results are the message
 602	
 603			case OutcomeSuccess:
 604				// The model has nothing more to call, so it believes it is done.
 605				// That is the moment to check, if the project asked us to.
 606				report, ok := c.runAutoCheck(ctx)
 607				if !ok {
 608					return
 609				}
 610				message = report
 611	
 612			case OutcomeInterrupted:
 613				next, keepGoing := c.afterInterrupt()
 614				if !keepGoing {
 615					return
 616				}
 617				c.accumulateInterrupt(next)
 618				message = next
 619	
 620			case OutcomeLooping:
 621				next, keepGoing := c.afterLoop()
 622				if !keepGoing {
 623					return
 624				}
 625				c.accumulateInterrupt(next)
 626				message = next
 627	
 628			default:
 629				return
 630			}
 631		}
 632	}

 634	// accumulateInterrupt saves the content of a send that was stopped before the
 635	// next send resets it, so the transcript can show the full arc of a steered
 636	// turn: what the model was saying, the steer, and the final answer.
 637	//
 638	// The steer is included when the user typed a custom correction rather than
 639	// choosing "Continue" (which carries no user text). A blockquote prefix makes
 640	// the authorship unambiguous in the markdown transcript.
 641	func (c *Coder) accumulateInterrupt(steer string) {
 642		if c.partialResponseContent != "" {
 643			c.turnHistory += c.partialResponseContent + "\n\n"
 644		}
 645		if steer != "" {
 646			c.turnHistory += "> " + strings.ReplaceAll(steer, "\n", "\n> ") + "\n\n"
 647		}
 648	}

 650	// sendSteerable runs one send under a context of its own, so that stopping the
 651	// send does not have to mean ending the turn.
 652	//
 653	// This is the whole of the change that makes steering possible. Ctrl-C used to
 654	// cancel the *turn's* context: everything downstream saw Canceled from then on,
 655	// and there was no way back into the loop even though the conversation itself
 656	// had survived intact. A child context per send moves the blast radius to the
 657	// one send, and the turn context stays live to make the next one.
 658	//
 659	// The tool calls of a send run inside it too — applyToolCalls takes this same
 660	// context — so Ctrl-C still kills a bash command that is running, which is the
 661	// property worth not losing.
 662	func (c *Coder) sendSteerable(ctx context.Context, message string) (SendOutcome, string) {
 663		sctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(ctx)
 664		c.sendMu.Lock()
 665		c.cancelSend = cancel
 666		c.sendMu.Unlock()
 667	
 668		defer func() {
 669			c.sendMu.Lock()
 670			c.cancelSend = nil
 671			c.sendMu.Unlock()
 672			cancel()
 673		}()
 674	
 675		return c.sendMessage(sctx, message)
 676	}

 678	// InterruptSend stops the send in flight without ending the turn.
 679	//
 680	// Called from the REPL's signal handler, which used to cancel the turn context
 681	// directly. A Ctrl-C between sends finds no send to cancel and does nothing,
 682	// which is correct: there is nothing in flight, and the prompt the user is
 683	// about to get asked is the interrupt they wanted.
 684	func (c *Coder) InterruptSend() {
 685		c.sendMu.Lock()
 686		cancel := c.cancelSend
 687		c.sendMu.Unlock()
 688		if cancel != nil {
 689			cancel()
 690		}
 691	}

 693	// settleEdits commits the turn's edits so far and records a snapshot to undo
 694	// them by.
 695	//
 696	// Factored out of the turn-end defer because an interruption is also a place
 697	// this belongs. The human stopped to look at something, which makes that point
 698	// a review boundary: `git show` gives exactly what the model did before it was
 699	// stopped, separately from what it did after the correction, and /undo steps
 700	// through the two halves one at a time. Anyone who wanted one commit has
 701	// /squash.
 702	//
 703	// What is *not* here is flushTurnUsage. The spend is a property of the turn,
 704	// not of each leg of it, so it stays in the defer and reports once.
 705	func (c *Coder) settleEdits(message string) {
 706		// Nothing written since the last settle, so there is nothing to settle.
 707		// Without this an interrupted-then-steered turn settles twice over the same
 708		// edits: the second commit finds the tree already matching HEAD and
 709		// announces "the turn left the files as they were", which is true of the
 710		// second attempt and false of the turn.
 711		//
 712		// turnSnap is the right signal rather than turnEditedFiles, which
 713		// accumulates across the whole turn because the history record at turn end
 714		// wants every file the turn touched. turnSnap is emptied by
 715		// pushTurnSnapshot and rebuilt by recordWrites, so it means precisely
 716		// "written since the last settle".
 717		if c.turnSnap.empty() {
 718			return
 719		}
 720		c.commitTurn(message)
 721		c.pushTurnSnapshot()
 722	}

 724	// afterInterrupt asks the human what a stopped turn should do next, and
 725	// reports the message to resume with and whether to resume at all.
 726	//
 727	// The choice is put through the Asker port, which is what ask_user_question
 728	// already uses to prompt in the middle of a turn — so this is a shape the
 729	// terminal handling has been driving all along rather than a new one. Free text
 730	// comes back as the raw line, which *is* the correction, so there is nothing to
 731	// parse. A nil Asker means no interactive terminal (script mode): stopping is
 732	// the only honest answer there, and it is what an interrupt has always done.
 733	//
 734	// The --yes flags deliberately do not answer this. They skip permission
 735	// prompts, and being asked what you meant by stopping is not a permission
 736	// prompt — the same line the port's own documentation draws for
 737	// ask_user_question.
 738	func (c *Coder) afterInterrupt() (message string, keepGoing bool) {
 739		if c.Asker == nil {
 740			return "", false
 741		}
 742		// The edits so far belong to the interrupt, whichever way this goes.
 743		c.settleEdits("")
 744	
 745		answer := c.Asker.Ask(AskRequest{
 746			Question: "You stopped the model. What now?",
 747			Options: []AskOption{
 748				{Label: "Continue", Description: "Carry on from where it was cut off"},
 749				{Label: "Stop", Description: "End the turn here"},
 750			},
 751		})
 752		if len(answer) == 0 {
 753			return "", false
 754		}
 755		switch answer[0] {
 756		case "Continue":
 757			// Say what the user decided, or the model is answering the wrong
 758			// question.
 759			//
 760			// noteInterrupt runs before this prompt, so all it can say is that the
 761			// reply was cut off. On its own that reads as a full stop, and the
 762			// model obliges: "No problem — I'll stop here. What would you like me
 763			// to do next?" It is not misreading anything. Asked afterwards what it
 764			// had been told, it quoted the cut-off note and said no continue choice
 765			// had reached it, which was exactly right.
 766			//
 767			// The rest of the wording closes the other failure mode. With a whole
 768			// partial reply above it and no instruction about what to do with it, a
 769			// model will also quite reasonably begin again from the top — which is
 770			// what an earlier live pass showed, and what was wrongly written up as
 771			// the cost of keeping the partial rather than as this bug.
 772			c.curMessages = append(c.curMessages, llm.HarnessNote(
 773				"The user chose to continue. Pick up exactly where your reply above "+
 774					"stops and carry on from there — do not start over, do not repeat "+
 775					"or summarize what you already wrote, and do not ask what to do next."))
 776			// The notes are the message, so the next send re-enters on them rather
 777			// than appending an empty user turn to carry nothing.
 778			c.resumeInPlace = true
 779			return "", true
 780		case "Stop":
 781			return "", false
 782		default:
 783			// Anything else the user typed is the steer, and it goes in as their
 784			// own words in their own voice. They really did type it.
 785			return answer[0], true
 786		}
 787	}

 789	// afterLoop asks what to do about a reply the harness stopped for repeating
 790	// itself, and reports whether the turn should continue.
 791	//
 792	// Its own function rather than a branch of afterInterrupt, because both halves
 793	// differ. The question cannot say "you stopped the model" — the user did not —
 794	// and "Continue" cannot mean "pick up exactly where your reply stops", which
 795	// here is an instruction to resume the loop. What is offered instead is a
 796	// retry: the loop's note (send.go) tells the model to take a different
 797	// approach, and the most useful thing the user can do is type what that should
 798	// be, which the free-text steer already carries.
 799	func (c *Coder) afterLoop() (message string, keepGoing bool) {
 800		if c.Asker == nil {
 801			return "", false
 802		}
 803		// The edits so far belong to the stopped reply, whichever way this goes.
 804		c.settleEdits("")
 805	
 806		answer := c.Asker.Ask(AskRequest{
 807			Question: "The model was repeating itself and was stopped. What now?",
 808			Options: []AskOption{
 809				{Label: "Stop", Description: "End the turn here"},
 810				{Label: "Try again", Description: "Let it answer again, told not to repeat itself"},
 811			},
 812		})
 813		if len(answer) == 0 {
 814			return "", false
 815		}
 816		switch answer[0] {
 817		case "Stop":
 818			return "", false
 819		case "Try again":
 820			// The note noteLoop already appended is the whole message: it says what
 821			// was stopped and what to do instead, so the next send re-enters on it
 822			// rather than appending an empty user turn to carry nothing.
 823			c.resumeInPlace = true
 824			return "", true
 825		default:
 826			// Anything else the user typed is the steer, in their own voice.
 827			return answer[0], true
 828		}
 829	}

 831	// runAutoCheck runs the project's check_auto checks at the end of a turn that
 832	// edited files, and reports whether the turn should continue.
 833	//
 834	// It fires here rather than after each edit because a mid-turn state is
 835	// legitimately broken: edit one file, then its caller, and in between nothing
 836	// compiles. Checking there would spend budget on failures the model was already
 837	// about to fix. At turn end the model has declared itself finished, which is
 838	// exactly when an independent check is worth something — and the reason to make
 839	// it independent is that the model's judgement about *which* check mattered is
 840	// the part that fails. A run that passed the tests and never linted still
 841	// reports "the checks pass".
 842	//
 843	// The returned message is a user turn, not a tool result, which is a deliberate
 844	// exception to the rule that reflection is a tool error. There is no call to
 845	// answer here: the model did not ask for this, the harness is speaking
 846	// unprompted, and a user message is the honest shape for that.
 847	func (c *Coder) runAutoCheck(ctx context.Context) (message string, keepGoing bool) {
 848		// Nothing changed since the last run — either the turn edited nothing at
 849		// all, or the model replied to a failure without touching a file, which is
 850		// a considered answer ("that isn't mine") and not something to re-ask.
 851		if len(c.CheckAuto) == 0 || !c.editedSinceCheck {
 852			return "", false
 853		}
 854		c.editedSinceCheck = false
 855		if c.autoChecks >= maxAutoCheck {
 856			c.Out.Warningf("The automatic checks have run %d times without passing; stopping here.", maxAutoCheck)
 857			return "", false
 858		}
 859		c.autoChecks++
 860	
 861		c.Out.Toolf("Running the automatic checks.")
 862		transcript, passed := c.runChecks(ctx, c.CheckAuto)
 863		if passed {
 864			return "", false
 865		}
 866		// The wording matters, and live testing is what showed why. "did not pass
 867		// after your changes" reads as "you caused this", which puts the model
 868		// between this message and the standing instruction to leave unrelated code
 869		// alone. Observed: it declined to fix a pre-existing failure, was asked
 870		// again by the next round, and gave in — two rounds spent on an argument the
 871		// harness started. Saying plainly that reporting is an acceptable answer
 872		// settles it in one.
 873		return "The automatic checks ran after your changes and did not pass:\n\n" + transcript +
 874			"\nIf this is something you broke, fix it. If it was already failing and is unrelated to " +
 875			"what you changed, say so and stop — don't fix it unless the user asks.", true
 876	}

 878	// confirmMoreSteps is the budget checkpoint. A long turn is legitimate, but it
 879	// should not run away unnoticed, so the user is shown what it has done so far
 880	// and asked whether to keep going. Declining ends the turn normally, with the
 881	// work up to that point already applied and committed. Answering yes buys
 882	// another MaxSteps.
 883	func (c *Coder) confirmMoreSteps() bool {
 884		files := len(c.turnEditedFiles)
 885		noun := "files"
 886		if files == 1 {
 887			noun = "file"
 888		}
 889		c.Out.Printf("This turn has run %d steps and edited %d %s.", c.numSteps, files, noun)
 890		if c.costKnown {
 891			c.Out.Printf("Cost so far: $%s.", formatCost(c.messageCost))
 892		}
 893	
 894		res := c.Confirm.Confirm(ConfirmRequest{Prompt: "Keep going?", Grant: GrantSteps})
 895		if !res.Yes {
 896			c.Out.Printf("Stopping here. The work so far is applied; say what to do next.")
 897			return false
 898		}
 899		c.numSteps = 0
 900		c.autoChecks = 0
 901		c.editedSinceCheck = false
 902		return true
 903	}

 959	// StreamReasoning renders the model's thinking, plain.
 960	//
 961	// It used to be an empty function, so `strument -m … > transcript.txt` dropped
 962	// the whole reasoning trace without saying so, while the same session run
 963	// interactively showed it. Which mode you happened to use decided whether the
 964	// thinking existed — a decision nobody made, and one that cost several live
 965	// runs chasing a marker that could not appear. How much to show is now
 966	// reasoning_display's to answer, in both modes alike.

 15	// The code tool: the model writes one small program and it runs in Monty, a
 16	// restricted Python interpreter compiled to WebAssembly (internal/monty). Two
 17	// measured facts motivate it (doc/plans/code-mode.md): arithmetic costs a
 18	// quarter of the reasoning lines in this repository's own experiments, and
 19	// models spend full request round trips on runs of read-only calls a program
 20	// could make in one step. This file is both halves — pure computation, and
 21	// the read-only bridge.

 24	// model writing ordinary Python will hit walls, and the description is the
 25	// only thing that can prevent most of them. The list of what is missing is
 26	// empirical — probed against the vendored monty.wasm, not read off upstream's
 27	// docs — and each wall a model hits anyway returns Monty's own error text,
 28	// which names the construct.

152	// codeOptions assembles the Execute options: the resource limits, plus the
153	// read-only bridge.
154	func (c *Coder) codeOptions() []monty.ExecuteOption {
155		opts := make([]monty.ExecuteOption, 0, 2)
156		opts = append(opts, monty.WithLimits(codeLimits))
157	
158		names := InspectorTools()
159		funcs := make([]monty.FuncDef, 0, len(names))
160		// Each tool takes its arguments as keywords; the params list is what lets
161		// Monty map a positional call's arguments onto those names. The schemas
162		// differ per tool (path, pattern, limit, …), so the program passes
163		// everything by name and Monty hands over whatever it got — an argument
164		// this side does not recognize is answered by the tool itself, exactly as
165		// a direct call with a wrong field would be.
166		for _, n := range names {
167			funcs = append(funcs, monty.Func(n))
168		}
169		opts = append(opts, monty.WithExternalFunc(c.bridgeCall(names), funcs...))
170		return opts
171	}

173	// bridgeCall is the ExternalFunc that pauses the program and answers one
174	// read-only tool call. It is an adapter, not a reimplementation: the call
175	// crosses the boundary as JSON and is answered by the same Inspector.Run a
176	// direct tool call goes through, so what the program sees is byte-for-byte
177	// what the model would have seen.
178	func (c *Coder) bridgeCall(allowed []string) monty.ExternalFunc {
179		isAllowed := make(map[string]bool, len(allowed))
180		for _, n := range allowed {
181			isAllowed[n] = true
182		}
183	
184		calls := 0
185		return func(_ context.Context, call *monty.FunctionCall) (any, error) {
186			// Fail closed. This runs behind the registration check already — a
187			// name outside `allowed` is not registered with Monty at all and
188			// raises NameError inside the program — but the check lives here too
189			// so the invariant does not depend on the registration list staying
190			// in step with it.
191			if !isAllowed[call.Name] {
192				return nil, fmt.Errorf("unknown function %q: only the read-only tools "+
193					"(%s) can be called from a program", call.Name, strings.Join(allowed, ", "))
194			}
195			calls++
196			if calls > maxBridgedCalls {
197				return nil, fmt.Errorf("the program made more than %d tool calls; "+
198					"stop and do the rest with direct tool calls", maxBridgedCalls)
199			}
200	
201			// Announce exactly as a direct call would be, so the review surface
202			// looks the same whether the model called read directly or from inside
203			// a program.
204			c.Out.Toolf("‹code› %s", call.Name)
205			tc := llm.ToolCall{Name: call.Name, Arguments: call.ArgsJSON()}
206			return c.inspector().Run(call.Name, tc.Arguments), nil
207		}
